identity: Qur'anic scripture: the Basmala followed by the complete text of Surat al-Qadr (surah 97, five ayat), in the Uthmani orthography of the standard mushaf (أنزلنه for أنزلناه, الملئكة for الملائكة, سلم for سلام, هى for هي, فى for في). Verse markers and all punctuation have been stripped, and the surah arrives as a single unbroken paragraph with no <NL> tokens at all, so the only free boundary in the document is the final token. 34 tokens, indices 0 to 33.
law: Verse-indexed scripture, doctrine section M: the unit is the aya, not the sentence and not the clause. In the Qur'an this is the strongest form of that law anywhere in the corpus, because the aya division is canonical and fixed rather than an editor's choice, so it is recoverable with certainty rather than guessed from prose rhythm. Here the verse law and the plain printed-sentence law agree at every site, since each aya of al-Qadr is also a complete self-standing sentence, and that convergence is why I sit at high confidence almost throughout instead of hedging as section M usually forces me to. Ahead of aya 1 the Basmala is its own segment. Result: six segments, Basmala plus five ayat, averaging about 5.7 tokens each. Note that this short unit is a property of this surah, not a base rate I may export (LAW 0 as revised: a frequency is never a law).
reasoning: Site 3, end of the Basmala, cut before إنا. The absence of any <NL> means the source flattened the surah onto one line, so I cannot lean on layout the way section A3 lets me for colophons and credit lines. The cut survives on two independent grounds anyway. Syntactically the Basmala is a self-contained formula, a bare prepositional phrase over a genitive chain with an elided verb, while إنا أنزلنه opens a complete verbal sentence carrying its own subject pronoun and object suffix; nothing binds the two. Typographically the Basmala is delimited in every rendering of every surah except al-Fatiha, and whatever mark carried that delimitation is exactly what the punctuation-stripping step deleted, which is the situation LAW 0-prime describes when it counts a layout-final mark as a boundary. HI. -- Site 8, القدر, end of aya 1, cut before وما. LAW 1 as revised says و is never by itself a reason to cut, and I have burned dozens of false cuts learning that; this cut is therefore not made on the و. It is made because إنا أنزلنه فى ليلة القدر is a completed proposition and وما أدريك ما ليلة القدر is the fixed Qur'anic rhetorical-question formula that always constitutes an aya of its own. Section M shows the gold cutting at verse starts that begin with و (Matthew 20:19, ويسلمونه إلى الأمم, opens a verse), so a و standing at a verse joint is evidence neither for nor against; the verse index decides, and it falls here. HI. -- Site 13, القدر, end of aya 2, cut before ليلة القدر خير. Asyndetic, and LAW 3 warns me twice over here: asyndetic repetition is not by itself a cut (T3 is dead), and a repeated NP is often apposition, which welds. This is not apposition. وما أدريك ما ليلة القدر is a complete interrogative and ليلة القدر خير من ألف شهر is a complete nominal sentence, mubtada plus khabar, that answers it. LAW 3's corrected discriminator asks whether each element was a complete printed sentence rather than whether the elements are parallel, and both of these are complete printed sentences carrying their own verse numbers. HI. -- Site 19, شهر, end of aya 3, cut before تنزل. Asyndetic again. تنزل الملئكة والروح introduces a new verbal sentence with a brand-new subject and a new event, after the comparison خير من ألف شهر has closed the preceding nominal sentence. Standard aya division. HI. -- Site 28, أمر, end of aya 4, cut before سلم. This is the only genuinely contested site in the document and it is the classic waqf dispute of this surah. Reading A takes سلم as a fresh mubtada: من كل أمر, then سلم هى حتى مطلع الفجر, peace it is until daybreak. Reading B takes سلم as a genitive attribute of أمر and moves the break one token later: من كل أمر سلم, then هى حتى مطلع الفجر. The standard Hafs an Asim numbering used by every printed mushaf ends aya 4 at أمر, which is Reading A, and an annotator working from a standard text inherits that division without having to adjudicate the tafsir question. I place the boundary at 28. I mark it MED rather than HI because this is precisely the LAW 5 failure shape that has cost me repeatedly, right sentence and wrong joint by one token, and because Reading B is a live and respectable alternative rather than something I invented to hedge. -- Site 33, الفجر, final token, mandatory and free. HI. -- Sites I deliberately did NOT cut. Index 15, the second القدر, sits inside ليلة القدر خير من ألف شهر as the subject NP of aya 3; cutting there would split a mubtada from its khabar. Index 22, والروح, is a و coordinating a second subject inside aya 4, and LAW 1 forbids treating it as a boundary. Indices 25 and 27, ربهم and كل, sit inside the prepositional tail بإذن ربهم من كل أمر, which LAW 4 keeps attached to its verb as a trailing adjunct. Aya 4 runs nine tokens with two coordinated subjects and two stacked prepositional phrases and is still one segment, which is exactly the shape section M told me to leave alone after eighty-seven false cuts inside verses in batch 2.
